english: I'd like a transit card, please
usage: Polite; said at a convenience store buying a T-money card
Add 하나 to specify a single card
Asking by brand name; 티머니 is the most common card
Where do I buy a transit card?
When you don't see them and need to ask
examples: 교통카드 주세요.
A transit card, please.
Said to a clerk at a GS25/CU convenience store counter
저기요, 티머니 카드 하나 주세요.
Excuse me, one T-money card, please.
티머니 is the brand; clerks understand it instantly
교통카드 사려고 하는데 여기서 팔아요?
I want to buy a transit card — do you sell them here?
사려고 하다 ('intending to buy') checks availability first
nuance: 교통카드 is 교통 ('transportation', Sino-Korean 交通) + 카드 ('card'), the generic word for the rechargeable tap card you use on every Korean subway and bus. In real life most people say the brand name 티머니 (T-money) — and 캐시비/Cashbee is the other big one — but 교통카드 is the safe umbrella term any clerk understands. You buy them at any convenience store (편의점) for a few thousand won, then load cash onto them. The key thing for English speakers: you do NOT buy single paper tickets for daily travel the way you might elsewhere — Koreans tap a reusable card, so asking for a 표 ('ticket') at a convenience store will confuse the clerk; ask for a 교통카드. Note also that 카드 alone often means a credit/debit card, so in a money context say 교통카드 in full to be clear. The polite default 주세요 is fine to a clerk; you would not use 반말 with a stranger behind a counter.

표 means a paper ticket, used for single-journey tokens or intercity buses — not everyday city travel. For tapping on/off the subway and bus, you buy a reusable 교통카드.
Saying just 카드 주세요 at a convenience store.
Bare 카드 is ambiguous and often means a credit card. To buy a transit card say the full 교통카드 주세요 (or 티머니 주세요).
Assuming the card is free or refundable like a deposit.
The plastic 교통카드 itself costs money (a few thousand won) and isn't refunded. Only the loaded cash balance is yours to spend; budget for the card price.

english: Please charge (load money on) my card
usage: Please load it / top it up
Polite; hand the card to a convenience-store clerk
State the amount before 충전; the most natural pattern
Asking whether this shop does T-money charging
How much shall I load for you?
What the clerk asks you back; reply with an amount
examples: 충전해 주세요.
Please top it up.
Said while placing your card on the counter
만 원만 충전해 주세요.
Just 10,000 won, please.
만 원만 ('only 10,000') sets a small, exact top-up
여기 교통카드 충전 돼요? 오천 원 충전해 주세요.
Can I charge a transit card here? Load 5,000 won, please.
Confirm the shop does it, then give the amount
nuance: 충전 is the Sino-Korean word (充電) literally meaning 'to charge (a battery)', but for a transit card it means 'to load cash onto it' — top it up. You say 충전해 주세요 to a convenience-store clerk, who taps your card on a pad and adds the cash you hand over; subway stations also have self-serve 충전 machines (교통카드 충전기). The natural order is amount + 충전해 주세요: 만 원 충전해 주세요 ('load 10,000 won'). For English speakers the trap is thinking 충전 means battery-charging only — it covers loading money, phone data, and gift balances too, so trust it here. Don't confuse 충전 (load money on) with 결제 ('payment/settling a charge') or 환불 ('refund'); they're different actions. Also note T-money is prepaid cash, so you must 충전 before the balance runs out — if it's empty the gate won't open. Use 주세요 (polite) with the clerk; the clerk uses honorific 드릴까요 ('shall I do for you?') back to you.

usage: Polite; asking a clerk to check your card balance
Could you check the balance, please?
Asking the clerk to read it for you
More casual everyday phrasing of the same question
examples: 잔액이 얼마예요?
How much balance is left?
Asked at the counter when you're unsure how much is on the card
저기요, 카드 잔액 좀 확인해 주세요.
Excuse me, could you check my card balance?
확인해 주세요 ('please check') asks the clerk to read it
아, 잔액 부족이래요. 충전해야겠어요.
Oh, it says low balance. I'd better top up.
Reacting to a 잔액 부족 beep before recharging
nuance: 잔액 is Sino-Korean (殘額) meaning 'remaining amount / balance'. You ask 잔액이 얼마예요? to find out how much cash is left on your transit card, and the dreaded gate beep 잔액 부족 ('insufficient balance') tells you it's too low to ride. A clerk can check it (잔액 확인), and so can the subway 충전 machines and many phone apps. The everyday casual alternative is 얼마 남았어요? ('how much is left?'), which is warmer and very common; 잔액이 얼마예요? is a touch more precise/formal because 잔액 is a financial noun. For English speakers the pitfall is the particle: it's 잔액이 얼마예요? (subject marker 이), not 잔액을 — you're not doing anything to the balance, you're stating that 'the balance is how much?'. Also don't mix up 잔액 (money left on a card) with 거스름돈 ('change' you get back from cash) — different concepts. When the gate flashes 잔액 부족, the fix is to step aside and 충전, not to push through.

Ignoring a 잔액 부족 beep and pushing through the gate.

usage: Polite-neutral; asking which numbered subway line
Asking the way to a specific line by number
Asking which line to board for your destination
Confirming what line you're currently on
examples: 강남역은 몇 호선이에요?
Which line is Gangnam Station on?
역 ('station') + 은, then ask the line number
시청 가려면 몇 호선 타야 돼요?
Which line do I take to get to City Hall?
가려면 ('in order to go') frames the route question
여기서 2호선으로 어떻게 가요?
How do I get to Line 2 from here?
2호선으로 ('toward Line 2') asks for directions to it
nuance: 호선 is the counter for numbered subway lines: 1호선 (Line 1), 2호선 (Line 2), and so on, where 호 (號) means 'number' and 선 (線) means 'line'. Crucially, line numbers use SINO-KOREAN numbers — 일, 이, 삼, 사… — so it's 이 호선 (2호선), NOT 두 호선; this is the single biggest learner slip because many counters take native numbers, but 호선 does not. You ask 몇 호선이에요? to learn which line a station is on, or 몇 호선 타야 돼요? to learn which to board. The particle for 'toward a line' is -으로/-로: 2호선으로 가요 ('go toward Line 2'). English speakers also tend to say 'Line number 2' literally as 라인 2 — Koreans never say 라인 for the subway; it's always 호선. Note named lines exist too (신분당선, 경의중앙선), which don't use 호선; for those you say the full name. To a stranger or station agent, keep it polite with -이에요/-예요; you wouldn't drop to 반말 asking directions.

Forcing 호선 onto named lines like 신분당선.

english: Does this go to City Hall Station?
usage: Does this go to City Hall Station?
Does this bus go to Gangnam?
Same pattern for a bus you're about to board
Is this subway heading toward Incheon?
Asking by 방향 ('direction') for which way it runs
To reach City Hall, do I take this one?
Confirming the right train with 타면 돼요
examples: 이거 시청역 가요?
Does this go to City Hall Station?
Asked to a fellow passenger or driver before boarding
저기요, 이 버스 서울역 가요?
Excuse me, does this bus go to Seoul Station?
To the bus driver as you step on; quick yes/no
이 지하철 강남 방향 맞아요?
Is this subway going the Gangnam direction, right?
맞아요? ('right?') asks them to confirm the direction
nuance: 이거 시청역 가요? is 이거 ('this one') + the destination + 가요? ('does it go?'), the everyday way to confirm a train or bus is heading where you want before you commit. The 가요 here is intransitive 'go (to)', and Korean often drops the destination particle in speech, so 시청역 가요? sounds natural without -에/-까지. For buses you swap 이거 for 이 버스, and the same frame works. The big subway-specific issue is DIRECTION: a single line runs both ways, so even on the right 호선 you can board the wrong way — that's why 방향 ('direction') questions like 강남 방향이에요? are so useful. English speakers tend to over-build this with 'go to' as 가는 거예요? or add 에 awkwardly (시청역에 가요?, which is fine but stiffer in this snap question); the crisp spoken form is just 시청역 가요?. Ask a fellow passenger, the driver, or a station agent — all polite -요 form; don't use 반말 with strangers. Note 가요? (does it go) differs from 내려요? (do I get off) — keep them distinct.

One line runs both ways. Even on the correct 호선, confirm direction: ask 강남 방향이에요? or 이거 시청역 가요? before getting on, or you'll ride away from your stop.

The natural spoken question drops particles: 이거 시청역 가요? Adding 에 (시청역에 가요?) is grammatical but stiffer for a quick boarding check.
Confusing 가요? (does it go) with 서요? (does it stop).
가요 asks the destination; 서요 (from 서다 'to stop') asks whether it stops at a place. For 'does this stop at City Hall?' say 시청역 서요?, not 가요?

usage: Polite-neutral; asking which stop is yours
Confirming this is the right stop
How many more stops to go?
Asking how far is left, by stop count
Please tell me when it's my stop
Asking the driver/passenger to alert you
examples: 남산 가려면 어디서 내려요?
To get to Namsan, where do I get off?
가려면 ('in order to go') sets up the get-off question
여기서 내리면 돼요? — 아니요, 다음이에요.
Should I get off here? — No, the next one.
Confirm with 내리면 돼요; reply names the right stop
기사님, 경복궁 가면 내릴 때 좀 알려 주세요.
Driver, please let me know when we reach Gyeongbokgung.
기사님 ('driver') + 알려 주세요 to be alerted on a bus
nuance: 어디서 내려요? is 어디서 ('at where', 어디 + the location-of-action particle 서) + 내려요 ('get off', from 내리다). This is the core question for not missing your stop. The particle 서 matters: getting off HAPPENS AT a place, so it's 어디서 내려요?, and 'get off here' is 여기서 내려요 — using 어디에 (static location) here is a classic English-speaker error, because 내리다 is an action that needs the dynamic 에서/서, not 에. The opposite verb is 타다 ('to get on/board'), and the pair 타다/내리다 is essential: you 타다 a vehicle and 내리다 from it. On buses, since stops aren't always announced clearly, 내릴 때 알려 주세요 ('tell me when it's my stop') asked to the 기사님 (driver) or a neighbor is genuinely useful. To confirm a specific stop, 여기서 내리면 돼요? ('is here where I get off?'). Keep it polite -요; you're addressing strangers or staff. Don't confuse 내리다 (get off a vehicle) with 떨어지다 ('to fall/drop') — only 내리다 fits exiting transit.

Mixing up 타다 (get on) and 내리다 (get off).
You 타다 onto a vehicle and 내리다 off it. Saying 어디서 타요? asks where to BOARD, not where to exit. For getting off, use 내리다: 어디서 내려요?
Saying 떨어져요? to mean 'get off'.
떨어지다 means 'to fall/drop'. To exit a bus or train, the verb is 내리다: 여기서 내려요. 떨어져요 would imply you physically fall off.

usage: Polite; asking the upcoming subway stop's name
Use 정류장 for buses instead of 역
이번 역 = the stop arriving now, vs 다음 = the one after
Is the next one City Hall, right?
Confirming the next stop by name
examples: 다음 역이 어디예요?
What's the next station?
Asked when you can't read or hear the announcement
저기요, 다음 정류장이 어디예요?
Excuse me, what's the next bus stop?
On a bus; 정류장 is the stop, not 역
이번 역이 강남역이에요? — 네, 이번이 강남이에요.
Is this station Gangnam? — Yes, this one's Gangnam.
이번 역 (arriving now) vs 다음 역 (the one after)
nuance: 다음 역이 어디예요? is 다음 ('next') + 역 ('station', Sino-Korean 驛) + 이 어디예요? ('is where/what?'). A subtle but crucial distinction trips up English speakers: 이번 역 means the station ARRIVING RIGHT NOW (announcements say 이번 역은… 'this stop is…'), while 다음 역 is the one AFTER that. So if you want the stop you're pulling into, ask 이번 역이 어디예요?; for the following one, 다음 역. Mixing them up makes you get off one stop early or late. The other key swap is 역 vs 정류장: 역 is a subway/train STATION, but a bus stop is a 정류장 (or 버스 정류장) — never call a bus stop a 역. The particle is 이 (subject): you're asking 'the next station is where?', so 역이 어디예요?, not 역을. 어디예요 literally asks 'where' but here naturally means 'which/what station'. Polite -요 is right for strangers and staff; this is a question you'd ask anyone nearby.

역 is a subway/train station. A bus stop is a 정류장. On a bus, ask 다음 정류장이 어디예요?, not 다음 역.

어디예요 takes a subject: 다음 역이 어디예요? You're asking 'the next station is where?', so mark it with 이, not the object 을.

english: Where do I go to transfer?
usage: Where do I go to transfer?
Polite; asking the way to a transfer point
Checking if this station allows a transfer
I want to transfer to Line 2
Stating the line you want to switch to
Asking for the 환승 통로 (connecting corridor)
examples: 환승하려면 어디로 가요?
Where do I go to transfer?
Asked to a station agent or passenger mid-journey
여기서 3호선으로 환승하고 싶은데 어디로 가요?
I want to transfer to Line 3 here — which way?
State target line, then ask the direction
버스에서 지하철로 환승하면 할인돼요?
If I transfer from bus to subway, is it discounted?
할인돼요? checks the transfer fare discount

usage: Polite; confirming this is the transfer stop
반말, telling a friend where to switch
What staff/locals tell you, honorific 셔야
Which line do I change to?
Asking which line to switch onto
examples: 여기서 갈아타면 돼요?
Do I change here?
Confirming with a passenger before you step off
사당역에서 4호선으로 갈아타면 돼요.
You change to Line 4 at Sadang Station.
Stating where and to which line to switch
잠실에서 갈아타야 해요? — 네, 거기서 갈아타세요.

The particle on the place is 서 (여기서, 사당역에서) because the changing HAPPENS AT that station — an action, so 에서/서, not static 에. The line you switch TO takes 로/으로: 4호선으로 갈아타요. english: Did you tap your bus card?
usage: Honorific question, e.g. what a driver might ask
Do I tap when getting off too?
examples: 카드 찍었어요? — 네, 찍었어요.
Did you tap? — Yes, I tapped.
찍다 ('to tap/stamp') is the verb for touching the reader
저기요, 내릴 때도 카드 찍어야 돼요?
Excuse me, do I tap when getting off too?
Tap-out matters for the transfer discount and distance fare
뒷문으로 내릴 때 단말기에 카드 찍으세요.
Tap your card on the reader at the back door when you get off.

nuance: The verb for tapping a transit card is 찍다 — literally 'to stamp/press/dot' — so 'tap your card' is 카드(를) 찍다, and the reader is the 단말기. This is THE word; English speakers often reach for 대다 ('to touch/put against', also heard: 카드를 대다) which is acceptable, but 찍다 is the idiomatic default everyone uses. Critically, on Korean city buses you tap TWICE: once boarding (front door) and AGAIN when getting off (back door) — the tap-out (하차 태그) is what preserves your 환승 할인 and charges the correct distance-based fare. Forgetting to tap out can cost you the transfer discount or a penalty fare next ride, so 내릴 때도 찍어야 돼요? ('do I tap getting off too?') — yes. The honorific 찍으셨어요? (with 시) is how a driver or elder addresses you; you'd answer plainly 찍었어요. Don't confuse 찍다 here with its other meanings (take a photo 사진을 찍다, dip food 찍어 먹다) — context makes it clear, but the action on the reader is 찍다. Buses also accept the same 교통카드 as the subway; you don't need a separate 'bus card'.

english: Can I pay with cash too?
usage: Can I pay with cash too?
Polite; asking the bus driver if cash is accepted
I don't have a card — does cash work?
Important: buses often give no change
examples: 현금도 돼요?
Can I pay cash too?
Asked to the driver as you board without a card
카드가 안 돼서 그러는데, 현금 내도 돼요?
My card isn't working, so — can I pay cash?
안 돼서 그러는데 ('since it's not working') softens the ask
버스는 현금 내면 거스름돈 안 줘요?
On the bus, if I pay cash, no change is given?
Confirming the no-change reality of cash bus fare
nuance: 현금 is Sino-Korean (現金) for 'cash', and 현금도 돼요? = 'does cash work too?' (되다 'to be possible' + the particle 도 'also/too'). You ask this mainly on BUSES, because a real-life gotcha is that paying cash on a Korean city bus often gives NO change (거스름돈) — you drop the exact fare in the box, and overpaying is simply lost. Subways take cash via ticket machines that DO give change, but buses typically don't, so 거스름돈 줘요? ('do I get change?') is a smart follow-up. The particle 도 ('too/also') implies 'cash, in addition to card' — natural when card is the default and you're checking the alternative; if you just ask 현금 돼요? (with no 도) that's also fine. To say HOW you'll pay, use 으로: 현금으로 낼게요 ('I'll pay by cash'), 카드로 낼게요 ('by card'). English speakers misuse 돈 ('money') for 'cash' — 돈 is money in general; specifically physical cash is 현금. Don't say 돈으로 돼요? when you mean cash; say 현금으로. Polite -요 with the driver.

usage: Polite; asking the location of a bus stop
Which numbered bus should I take?
Asking which bus by route number
Do I board at this stop?
Confirming this is the right stop to board
examples: 저기요, 버스 정류장이 어디예요?
Excuse me, where's the bus stop?
Asked to a passerby on the street
강남역 가는 버스 정류장이 어디예요?
Where's the stop for the bus to Gangnam Station?
가는 ('that goes') specifies which bus's stop
146번은 어느 정류장에서 타요?
Which stop do I catch the 146 at?
버스 번호 + 어느 정류장에서 타요 for the boarding stop

To say at which stop you board, use 에서 (the action-location particle): 이 정류장에서 타요 ('I board at this stop'), because boarding is an action. usage: How long do I have to wait?
examples: 이 버스 자주 와요?
Does this bus come often?
Asked to someone waiting at the same stop
146번 배차 간격이 어떻게 돼요?
What's the interval for the 146?
배차 간격 is the gap between buses on a route
다음 버스 언제 와요? 앱에는 10분이라는데.
When's the next bus? The app says 10 minutes.

usage: Polite; asking the last departure time
언제 ('when') variant of the same question
첫차 ('first train/bus') — the opposite of 막차
Has the last one already gone?
Asking if service has ended for the night
examples: 막차 몇 시예요?
What time's the last train?
Asked late at night to a station agent or driver
지하철 막차 몇 시예요? 자정 전에 끊겨요?
When's the last subway? Does it stop before midnight?

막차 놓치면 택시 타야 돼요.

('has the last one already gone?') — note 끊기다 here doesn't mean a phone call dropping; it means the line/service has stopped for the night. To say you MISSED it, use 놓치다 ('to miss/let slip'): 막차 놓쳤어요 ('I missed the last train'). Time uses 시 with NATIVE numbers for the hour (열두 시 'twelve o'clock'), but minutes use Sino-Korean — a frequent learner mix-up. Polite -요 with staff.

usage: Polite; checking if a seat is taken
Checking if the spot is occupied by someone
examples: 이 자리 비었어요?
Is this seat free?
Asked to a nearby passenger before sitting
여기 사람 있어요? — 아니요, 앉으세요.
Is anyone here? — No, please sit.
Common exchange; 앉으세요 ('please sit') invites you
죄송한데, 여기 노약자석이에요.
Sorry, but this is a priority seat.
노약자석 ('elderly/disabled seat') — leave it for those who need it
nuance: 이 자리 비었어요? is 이 자리 ('this seat') + 비었어요? (past of 비다 'to be empty'), literally 'is this seat empty?' — the polite way to check before sitting. The most natural alternatives are 여기 사람 있어요? ('is anyone here?', checking for an occupant) and 여기 앉아도 돼요? ('may I sit here?', asking permission). A cultural must-know: Korean subways/buses have 노약자석 (priority seats for the elderly, pregnant, disabled) usually at the car ends, and 임산부 배려석 (pink pregnant-passenger seats) — even if empty, a young able-bodied person is strongly expected NOT to sit there, so 이 자리 비었어요? doesn't override that etiquette. The verb 비다 ('be empty') here is intransitive; English speakers sometimes use 자유 ('freedom') literally for 'free' (이 자리 자유예요?) which is nonsense in Korean — 'free/vacant' for a seat is 비다 (empty) or 'no one here' (사람 없어요). Also 비었어요 (empty/vacant) vs 없어요 ('there isn't'): 자리 없어요 means 'there are no seats (all full)', a different statement. Polite -요 with strangers; you'd never use 반말.

Sitting in 노약자석 or 임산부 배려석 when able-bodied.

Confusing 자리 비었어요 with 자리 없어요.
비었어요 ('it's empty/free') asks if THIS seat is open; 없어요 ('there isn't') means no seats are available at all. They're nearly opposite — keep them straight.

usage: Polite; squeezing past to reach the door
Said to make people step aside briefly
Announcing you need to exit, so people move
More direct request to clear the way
examples: 저기요, 좀 지나갈게요.
Excuse me, let me through.
Pushing toward the door on a crowded train
잠깐만요, 내릴게요!
One sec — I'm getting off!
잠깐만요 + 내릴게요 to part a packed crowd at your stop
죄송합니다, 좀 지나갈게요. 다음에 내려요.
Sorry, coming through — I get off next.
Apologize, state you're passing, give the reason
nuance: 좀 지나갈게요 is 좀 (softener) + 지나가다 ('to pass by/through') + -ㄹ게요 (announcing your own action politely), 'I'm going to pass through (so excuse me)'. On a packed Seoul subway this is the phrase that gets you to the door in time. The single most useful crowd word is actually 잠깐만요 ('just a moment'), said to make people shift aside — it's gentler than a command. To announce you're EXITING so people clear the path, say 내릴게요 ('I'm getting off!'), which is hugely effective at your stop. A more direct option is 좀 비켜 주세요 ('please step aside'), slightly stronger. English speakers wrongly use 실례합니다 ('pardon the intrusion') here — it's understandable but stiff/formal for a quick squeeze; Koreans say 잠깐만요 or 좀 지나갈게요. Also don't translate 'excuse me' as 미안해요 (an apology for wrongdoing) when you just need to pass — though 죄송합니다 can accompany the squeeze. The -ㄹ게요 ending signals intent and courtesy at once. Keep it polite -요; you're brushing past strangers, so the softener 좀 and the -요 ending matter a lot.

Saying 미안해요 alone when you mean 'excuse me, let me by'.

usage: Polite-neutral; checking if a train skips stops
Is this train express or all-stop?
Does the express stop at City Hall?
I should take the regular train
examples: 이거 급행이에요?
Is this the express?
Asked on the platform before boarding a 1호선 train
급행 타면 우리 역 안 서요?
If I take the express, won't it stop at our station?
안 서요 ('doesn't stop') — the express skips it
급행 놓쳤는데 다음 일반 열차 언제 와요?
I missed the express — when's the next regular train?
일반/완행 ('all-stop') as the slower alternative
nuance: 급행 is Sino-Korean (急行) meaning 'express', a train that skips many stations to run faster — found on lines like 1호선, 9호선, 경의중앙선, and 수인분당선. Its opposite is 완행 or, more commonly said, 일반 (열차) ('regular/all-stop train'). The make-or-break point for newcomers: a 급행 will BLOW PAST your station if it's not an express stop, so before boarding you ask 이거 급행이에요? and, vitally, 급행 우리 역 서요? ('does the express stop at my station?'). The verb for stopping is 서다 (서요 / 안 서요), distinct from 가다 ('to go') — 급행이 안 서요 means 'the express doesn't stop (here)', which is exactly what catches people out. 9호선 in particular runs 급행 and 일반 on the same tracks, and tourists routinely overshoot. English speakers sometimes call it the 'express' in English to staff or reach for 빠른 기차 ('fast train') — the correct term is 급행; 빠른 기차 isn't how the system is labeled. Signs and announcements mark trains 급행 vs 일반, so learn to recognize 급행. Polite -요 with staff and passengers.

Using 가다 instead of 서다 to ask about stopping.
급행 시청역 가요? asks the destination; to ask if it STOPS there, use 서다: 급행 시청역 서요? The express may 'go' that direction yet not 'stop' at your station.
Calling it 빠른 기차 instead of 급행.
The system labels fast trains 급행 (express) vs 일반/완행 (all-stop). 빠른 기차 ('fast train') is understandable but not the real term; say 급행이에요?

usage: Polite; asking someone near the button to press it
Checking the stop has been requested
You press the bell to get off
하차벨 ('alighting bell') — bus won't stop otherwise
I'll get off next, I'll press the bell
examples: 벨 눌러 주세요!
Please press the bell!
Asking a passenger by the button when you can't reach it
내릴 거면 미리 벨 눌러요.
If you're getting off, press the bell ahead of time.
미리 ('in advance') — press before the stop, not at it
벨 안 누르면 그냥 지나가요.
If you don't press the bell, it just drives past.
Buses skip stops with no bell and no waiting riders
nuance: 벨 is the loanword 'bell' — the STOP-REQUEST BUTTON on a Korean city bus (formally 하차벨, 하차 'alighting' + 벨), and 벨 눌러 주세요 = 'please press the bell', using 누르다 ('to press') + the favor 주세요. This is essential because Korean buses do NOT stop at every stop automatically: if no one has pressed the bell AND no one is waiting at the stop, the driver drives straight past. So you must press the red 벨 in advance (미리) when your stop is coming. The verb is 누르다 ('to press a button'), conjugating 눌러요/눌러 주세요 (르-irregular) — don't use 찍다 (that's for tapping the card) or 치다 ('to hit') here; you 누르다 a button. If you're not near a button on a crowded bus, you can ask a fellow passenger 벨 좀 눌러 주세요. English speakers sometimes say 버튼 ('button'), which is understood, but the bus stop-request is idiomatically the 벨/하차벨. Note this is bus-specific — subways stop at every station, so there's no 벨 underground. Polite -요/주세요 with strangers; among friends 벨 눌러 (반말).
